headline: Acoustic mapping app uses old Android phones to hunt Shahed drones, creating a crowd-sourced defense network
summary: A Lithuanian startup developed an Android app that leverages thousands of networked phones to detect the acoustic signatures of Shahed-type drones, providing early warnings for civilians and military.
details: A Lithuanian startup has developed an Android app designed to detect Shahed-type drones by analyzing their unique acoustic signatures. The system utilizes a network of verified users' old Android phones, transforming them into a crowd-sourced early warning system against these low-cost, effective threats.

The app employs an embedded algorithm to isolate drone sounds from environmental noise, reporting potential detections on a public map. With enough devices, the system can approximate a drone's location and direction, providing crucial alerts to both civilians and defense forces.

Shahed drones are challenging for traditional radar systems due to their small size, lightweight materials, and low radar cross-section (RCS). Their low flight altitude also makes them difficult for ground-based radars to pick up unless they are very close.

However, their low flight path means they are often audible to ground observers. By collecting and centralizing these acoustic detections, defense forces can mobilize to intercept drones far from populated areas, leveraging a method reminiscent of World War I acoustic mirrors.

Unlike the older acoustic mirrors, this modern system uses advanced algorithms and thousands of distributed detectors for enhanced accuracy. While not a standalone solution, it significantly augments modern radar systems by providing an additional data source to confirm targets and reduce clutter.

headline_marked: [[Optimize your CLAUDE.md]] for peak AI performance: only include what prevents mistakes
headline: Optimize your CLAUDE.md for peak AI performance: only include what prevents mistakes
summary: Learn to craft an effective CLAUDE.md by focusing on essential project details and explicit instructions, avoiding redundant information that hinders Claude's performance and clarity.
details: A great CLAUDE.md file is concise, with every line directly influencing Claude's actions. The key is knowing precisely what to include and, crucially, what to omit to avoid bloat and improve performance.

Start with a brief project description, your tech stack, and specific version numbers. While Claude infers much from code, it won't guess framework versions or ORM choices, which are vital for accurate context.

Include a top-level directory map, noting what each section holds, along with build and test commands. Also, specify coding conventions not enforced by formatters and, critically, areas Claude should never modify.
Ruthlessly apply the "every line earns its place" rule: if removing a line won't cause Claude to make a mistake, delete it. This prevents a bloated file from burying important instructions in noise.

Avoid personality instructions like "act as a senior engineer" or "think step by step," as Claude already performs these functions. Also, don't restate rules already enforced by linters or formatters; integrate those tools via hooks instead.

A leaner CLAUDE.md improves Claude's reliability and performance. Since the file loads into Claude's context every session, a compact file ensures critical rules get the necessary attention without competing with filler.
